messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Rajesh's Collision

Rajesh Patel was fifty-eight when the accident happened, driving home from a community health initiative meeting on a Tuesday evening in November. The intersection on Elm and Third was familiar—he'd crossed it a thousand times. A delivery truck ran the red light at forty miles per hour, and the impact came from his left side with a violence that seemed to compress time itself. Metal screamed. Glass detonated inward. For three seconds that felt like an hour, Rajesh was suspended in a physics of destruction, his body thrown sideways against the driver's door, his head snapping back. When the car finally stopped, he hung there gasping, alive but convinced he was dying. The paramedics found him conscious but in profound shock, his left arm fractured in two places, his ribs cracked. The doctors said he was fortunate. He had survived. But something in him had not.

The first months were about healing the body—physical therapy, pain management, the slow reacquisition of movement. By spring, Rajesh could walk without a cane and had returned to his work as a program director at a nonprofit focused on immigrant mental health services. His colleagues welcomed him back gently. But something had shifted in the architecture of his perception. Unexpected sounds—a car horn, a door slamming, even the metallic clang of a dropped pot in the office kitchen—would send a jolt of electricity through his chest, his body tensing as if the truck were coming at him again. When his colleague Marcus mentioned a fender-bender in the parking lot, Rajesh felt his throat tighten, his mind flooding with images he could not control: the hood of his own car crumpling, the sensation of impact, the taste of blood. The conversation had triggered something visceral in him, and he excused himself to the bathroom, where he stood gripping the sink until his hands stopped shaking.

By summer, Rajesh had begun to notice a pattern that frightened him more than the symptoms themselves. Certain textures—the rough weave of his car's upholstery, the fabric of his office chair—would catch his attention and suddenly he was back in that intersection, his body flooded with the original terror, the memory arriving not as recollection but as present-moment reality. His heart would hammer. His breath would come shallow and fast. The memory felt photographic, visceral: he could see the truck's grille, the driver's shocked face, the spiderweb fracture in his windshield spreading like a living thing. When he tried to recall the event for the insurance claim, the terror came flooding back with undiminished intensity—not as a story he was telling, but as an experience he was reliving. And once the memory had seized him, he found himself hypervigilant, scanning the world for threats. Every unexpected movement in his peripheral vision—a pedestrian stepping off a curb, a cyclist approaching from behind—triggered a defensive startle, his body reacting before his mind could assess whether danger was real.

Rajesh had come to believe that his own mind was a danger to him. The textures, the sounds of traffic, even the sight of cars in certain angles of light—all of these had become harbingers of the memory, and the memory itself had become a kind of waking nightmare. He began to avoid driving whenever possible, which meant his wife Meera drove him to work, a reversal that embarrassed him. He stopped attending the monthly traffic safety committee meetings he had helped establish. When colleagues asked why, he could not explain the suffocating dread that rose in his chest at the thought of sitting in a room discussing accident prevention. He had started taking longer routes through the neighborhood to avoid the intersection, and he found himself unable to sit in the passenger seat without gripping the door handle, his leg muscles tense, ready to brace for impact. The hyperarousal had become constant—a low-level electricity in his nervous system that made sleep difficult and left him exhausted. Three years after the collision, Rajesh finally called a therapist, hoping that someone might help him understand why his own mind had become the thing he needed protection from.
